title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?

keyTerms.d: The confident modern assumption that faith and science are old enemies, locked in a long war — the church against Galileo, superstition against the telescope, dogma dragging its heels while reason advances. It is not ancient: it has a birthday, an author, and a sequel. Over the last half-century, historians of science — including many with no religious stake at all — have largely abandoned the “warfare” picture as bad history.

The two nineteenth-century bestsellers that built the conflict thesis: John William Draper’s History of the Conflict between Religion and Science (1874) and Andrew Dickson White’s A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom (1896). They were enormously influential — and, as history, largely wrong, as specialists now say bluntly. The imagery is older still (Jefferson, 1820, wrote that the priests “dread the advance of science as witches do the approach of day-light”).

The careful, contested claim that certain Christian theological convictions supplied intellectual preconditions that made the scientific enterprise thinkable (Hooykaas, Harrison). It is not that Christianity single-handedly manufactured science — the strong slogan “no Christianity, no science” overreaches badly — but that its picture of a rational, contingent, intelligible creation was fertile soil in which the enterprise could take root and last.

keyTerms.t: A free Creator — so you must go and look
keyTerms.d: The first of the three convictions. If God made the world by choice rather than necessity, then the world is contingent — it could have been otherwise — and you cannot deduce its workings by pure reason from your armchair, as the Greeks so often tried. You have to go and look. The other two convictions are an intelligible, ordered creation open to minds made in God’s image, and human fallibility — a fallen mind that must be checked, replicated, and disciplined against self-deception.

The “voluntarist” picture of God — tracing to Michael Foster (1934) and Francis Oakley (1961) — that Reijer Hooykaas argued underwrote the empirical turn: nature must be interrogated, not merely contemplated. The attribution is deliberately bounded: Peter Harrison has cautioned that the link is looser than the thesis claims, noting that leading voluntarists such as Descartes were not empiricists.

John Hedley Brooke’s framework: there is no single relationship between science and religion to be told as conflict or as harmony, only many particular entanglements, each to be studied in its own setting — a verdict that tells as much against a tidy Christian success story as against the warfare myth. Historians are wary of every tidy slogan here, and that wariness is exactly what makes their verdict on the warfare thesis worth trusting.

The honest bound this whole case keeps: that a worldview proved intellectually fruitful is not proof that it is correct. Good and true are different things. The case for the faith rests not on what it built but on whether Jesus rose from the dead, argued on its own evidence elsewhere in the Library. What the history dissolves is a barrier — the assumption that a thinking person must choose between the laboratory and the church — not a proof of the faith.

A genuine scar, owned without flinching. In 1616 the Roman Inquisition’s theologians judged heliocentrism “foolish and absurd in philosophy, and formally heretical,” and in 1633 Galileo was tried, made to abjure, and held under house arrest for life. The Roman Catholic authorities of that moment were wrong to condemn him and wrong to bind Scripture to one astronomy. But one tragedy is not a three-century war; the dispute cut across both church and academy; and the honest response is neither anti-Catholic point-scoring nor Protestant self-congratulation.

derive.q: Nearly all the founders of modern science — Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, Newton — studied nature because they believed it was God’s handiwork. Does that, by itself, prove the faith true?
derive.ans: no — it dissolves a barrier, it does not prove the faith
derive.why: None of it shows Christianity is true. That a worldview proved intellectually fruitful is not proof that it is correct; good and true are different things, and the case for the faith rests not on what it built but on whether Jesus rose from the dead, which is argued on its own evidence elsewhere. What the history does dissolve is a barrier: the widespread assumption that a thinking person must choose between the laboratory and the church.

derive.q: Historians have retired the “warfare” thesis. Who retired it — Christian apologists defending their own, or the mainstream of the discipline?
derive.ans: the mainstream — many of them with no religious stake
derive.why: The correction is not a fringe Christian complaint; it is the mainstream of the discipline. Ronald Numbers — himself no apologist for religion — edited the landmark collection in which twenty-five scholars dismantle the set-piece stories one by one, and that is exactly what makes the verdict against the warfare model worth trusting.

derive.q: The careful thesis says Christian convictions were fertile soil for science. Is that the same claim as “no Christianity, no science”?
derive.ans: no — that strong slogan overreaches badly
derive.why: Historians do not treat Christianity as a sufficient explanation, and the strong slogan “no Christianity, no science” overreaches badly. The modest thesis has real scholarly support: not that Christianity single-handedly manufactured science, but that its picture of a rational, contingent, intelligible creation was fertile soil in which the enterprise could take root and last.

derive.q: The Galileo affair was a real injustice, and this case concedes it. Does conceding it hand the warfare thesis the win?
derive.ans: no — one scar is not a war
derive.why: The Galileo affair is a genuine scar, and it should be owned without flinching. But one scar is not a war. In 1616 the evidence did not yet favour Copernicus, so the church sided with the scientific majority of the day — which is not a defence of the verdict, but it does explode the idea that faith was simply refusing an obvious fact; and the conflict ran across both church and academy, not along a tidy front of religion against reason.

derive.q: Modern science also stands on Greek mathematics and the Islamic Golden Age. Does that sink the Christian-preconditions claim?
derive.ans: no — the case needs no Christian monopoly
derive.why: Science was never a solely Christian achievement. It stands on Greek mathematics and logic, and on the Islamic Golden Age, when scholars in Baghdad, Cairo, and Córdoba preserved and advanced Greek learning, founded algebra, and — in Ibn al-Haytham’s optics — pioneered controlled experiment centuries before Europe. The case here neither needs nor claims a Christian monopoly.

honestState.p1: Two honest limits keep this argument where it belongs. First, the thesis that Christian theology supplied the preconditions of science is a claim about history, and a contested one; historians rightly resist any monocausal story, and Numbers’s own Galileo Goes to Jail counts “that Christianity gave birth to modern science” among its myths — a caution against replacing the old warfare story with a triumphalist inverse. Take it as the careful historians offer it: not that Christianity single-handedly manufactured science, but that its picture of a rational, contingent, intelligible creation was fertile soil in which the enterprise could take root and last. Second, science was never a solely Christian achievement — it stands on Greek mathematics and logic, and on the Islamic Golden Age.
honestState.fairness: The cautions here come from within the discipline, not from opponents of the faith. Ronald Numbers, no apologist for religion, counts “that Christianity gave birth to modern science” among the myths his own volume dismantles; John Hedley Brooke’s “complexity thesis” resists every tidy slogan — a Christian success story as much as the warfare myth; and Peter Harrison, one of the preconditions thesis’s own defenders, is also its sharpest critic on voluntarism. On the Galileo affair, Maurice Finocchiaro reads the conflict as running across church and academy alike; the Orthodox writer David Bentley Hart calls it less a war of science against faith than a collision of egos, personality, and politics; and on Giordano Bruno, Alberto Martinez argues his cosmology weighed more heavily in the condemnation than the standard account allows.
honestState.verdict: So the war is the modern invention. It is not a fact discovered by historians but a story popularised by two nineteenth-century writers, embraced because it flattered an age, and quietly retired by the scholars who checked it. In its place stands a scientific revolution midwifed in a Christian civilisation, by men who thought that in reading the book of nature they were reading a second scripture from the same hand — and whose convictions about a rational, contingent, intelligible creation were fertile soil for the enterprise. The Galileo affair is a genuine scar and should be owned without flinching; but one scar is not a war, and the case claims no Christian monopoly over learning that also runs through Greece and the Islamic Golden Age. And — this matters most — none of it shows Christianity is true. Fruitful and true are different things; the history dissolves a barrier, it does not prove the faith. That case rests on the resurrection, argued on its own evidence elsewhere.

order: The supposed war between science and Christian faith is a modern invention — the founders of modern science were overwhelmingly Christians who studied nature because they believed it was God’s handiwork, and modern specialists, many of them secular, have retired the “conflict thesis” as bad history.

Certain Christian theological convictions — a free Creator who made a contingent world you must go and look at, an intelligible ordered creation, and human fallibility that must be checked — supplied intellectual preconditions in which the enterprise could take root and last (the careful thesis, not “no Christianity, no science”; Greek and Islamic learning were indispensable too).

Therefore the assumption that a thinking person must choose between the laboratory and the church is false — modern science was born in a Christian context, not against it. This dissolves a barrier; it does not prove the faith is true, because fruitful and true are different things.

cards.a: The supposed war between science and Christian faith is a modern invention: the founders of modern science were overwhelmingly Christians who studied nature because they believed it was God’s handiwork, and modern specialists, many of them secular, have retired the “conflict thesis” as bad history.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and its precision check.
cards.a: Certain Christian theological convictions — a free Creator who made a contingent world you must go and look at, an intelligible ordered creation, and human fallibility that must be checked — supplied intellectual preconditions in which the scientific enterprise could take root and last. Precision: this is the careful thesis, NOT “no Christianity, no science” — historians do not treat Christianity as a sufficient explanation, and Greek and Islamic learning were indispensable too.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: It reaches that the assumption a thinking person must choose between the laboratory and the church is false — modern science was born in a Christian context, not against it. It does NOT reach that Christianity is true: fruitful and true are different things, so the history dissolves a barrier but proves nothing about the creed. The case for the faith rests on the resurrection, argued on its own evidence elsewhere.

cards.q: What are the three theological convictions in Premise 2?
cards.a: A free Creator who made the world by choice, so it is contingent and you must go and look rather than deduce it from your armchair; an intelligible, ordered creation open to minds made in God’s image; and human fallibility — a fallen mind that is not to be trusted alone, so knowledge must be checked, replicated, and disciplined against self-deception.

cards.q: Why doesn’t the Galileo affair prove a war between faith and science?
cards.a: Concede the injustice fully first: the Roman authorities were wrong to condemn him and wrong to bind Scripture to one astronomy. But in 1616 the evidence did not yet favour Copernicus — his system used circles and epicycles and predicted no better than Ptolemy, and Tycho’s system kept the earth still while fitting the same data, including the phases of Venus. The dispute cut across both church and academy. One tragedy is not a three-century war.

cards.q: What exactly was the church’s error in the Galileo affair — and what was it not?
cards.a: Its error was jurisdiction, not caution: it converted a legitimate scientific reservation into a charge of heresy and bound the reading of Scripture to a particular astronomy. It was NOT simply refusing an obvious fact. And it is no weapon for one branch of the church against another — the error was the Roman authorities’ of that moment, calling for a shared caution against mistaking the science of the hour for the word of God.

cards.q: How does the “fruitful is not true” firewall work?
cards.a: That a worldview grew science shows it was intellectually fertile; it never shows its claims are true — good and true are different things. Keep the two apart. The history dissolves a barrier (the idea you must choose between lab and church); whether the faith is true rests on whether Jesus rose from the dead, argued on its own evidence, not on the history of science.

cards.q: Who retired the warfare thesis — and why does that matter to the argument?
cards.a: The mainstream of the discipline retired it, many of them with no religious stake at all. That matters because the correction is not a fringe Christian complaint but the settled verdict of secular and believing historians alike — which is exactly what makes it worth trusting.

cards.q: What does the “complexity thesis” guard against?
cards.a: It holds that there is no single relationship between science and religion to be told as conflict or as harmony — only many particular entanglements, each studied in its own setting. It tells as much against a tidy Christian success story as against the warfare myth, keeping every side honest; that wariness is what makes the verdict on the warfare thesis trustworthy.

cards.q: Reply to: “Science was really a Greek and Islamic achievement, not a Christian one.”
cards.a: All true, and the case needs no Christian monopoly. Science stands on Greek mathematics and logic and on the Islamic Golden Age — Ibn al-Haytham’s optics pioneered controlled experiment centuries before Europe. The careful thesis is only that Christian convictions about a rational, contingent, intelligible creation were the fertile soil in which the self-sustaining enterprise took decisive root in early-modern Europe — offered alongside those debts, never against them.

cards.q: Reply to: “‘Science was born from Christianity’ is just the warfare myth flipped over.”
cards.a: Agreed, and the track states it in its own voice: historians resist any monocausal story, and “that Christianity gave birth to modern science” is itself counted among the myths a leading volume dismantles. Take it as the careful historians offer it — theological preconditions that made the enterprise thinkable and durable, a contested interpretation, not a demonstrated law of history.

cards.q: Reply to: “They were all believers only because everyone in Europe was baptised.”
cards.a: Granted — in a Europe where nearly everyone was baptised, the founders being members of the church would prove little on its own. What matters is not their membership but that so many of them said, in their own writings, that faith was their reason for looking.

obj.q: If the warfare thesis has one battle it can always name, it is Galileo. In 1616 the Inquisition’s theologians judged heliocentrism “foolish and absurd in philosophy, and formally heretical”; in 1633 Galileo was tried, made to abjure, and confined to house arrest for the rest of his life. That is faith crushing reason.
obj.model: Concede it fully first: this was a real injustice and a real error. The Roman Catholic authorities were wrong to condemn him, wrong to bind Scripture to a particular astronomy, wrong to silence a man for being — as it turned out — right; no account worth reading pretends otherwise. But the clean fable does not survive the details. In 1616 the evidence did not yet favour Copernicus: his system still used circles and epicycles and predicted no better than Ptolemy’s, and Tycho Brahe’s system fit the same data — including the phases of Venus — while keeping the earth still. The dispute cut across both church and academy (Jesuit astronomers confirmed Galileo’s observations; his fiercest opponents included secular Aristotelian professors). The church’s error was jurisdiction, not caution — it turned a legitimate scientific reservation into a charge of heresy. And this is no weapon for one branch of the church against another: the error was the Roman authorities’ of that moment, and the honest response is neither anti-Catholic point-scoring nor Protestant self-congratulation, but a shared caution against ever mistaking the science of the hour for the word of God. One Italian tragedy is not a three-century war.

obj.q: Grant the whole story. Then Christianity must be onto something true — a false worldview could not have been that intellectually fruitful. So the history of science is evidence that the faith is true.
obj.model: This one cuts toward us, and we still do not take it: fruitful is not true. A worldview can be intellectually productive without being correct — good and true are different things. What the history does is dissolve a barrier: the widespread assumption that a thinking person must choose between the laboratory and the church. Whether the faith is true rests on whether Jesus rose from the dead, argued on its own evidence elsewhere — not on the history of science. So the honest verdict is no: this proves the enemies were never at war; it does not prove the creed.

obj.q: Modern science stands on Greek mathematics and logic, and on the Islamic Golden Age — Baghdad, Cairo, Córdoba — where scholars preserved Greek learning, founded algebra as a discipline, and in Ibn al-Haytham pioneered controlled experiment centuries before Europe. Christianity gets undue credit.
obj.model: All true, and the case here neither needs nor claims a Christian monopoly. Science was never a solely Christian achievement: it stands on Greek mathematics and on the Islamic Golden Age, and Ibn al-Haytham’s optics is a landmark of controlled experiment. The careful thesis is only that Christian convictions about a rational, contingent, intelligible creation were the fertile soil in which the self-sustaining enterprise took decisive root in early-modern Europe — an interpretation offered alongside those debts, never against them.

obj.q: This is the old warfare myth flipped over — a tidy Christian slogan where there was a tidy anti-Christian one. History has no single cause, and “no Christianity, no science” is as crude as what it replaces.
obj.model: Agreed, and the track states it in its own voice: historians do not treat Christianity as a sufficient explanation, and the slogan “no Christianity, no science” overreaches badly. Numbers’s own Galileo Goes to Jail counts “that Christianity gave birth to modern science” among its myths, a caution against replacing the old warfare story with a triumphalist inverse. Take it as the careful historians — Hooykaas, Harrison — offer it: theological preconditions that made the enterprise thinkable and durable, a contested interpretation, not a demonstrated law of history.

unseen.q: Christianity is structurally anti-science. It teaches that the Bible is the final authority on everything, so whenever Scripture and the world collide — Genesis against astronomy, against biology — faith is bound to override the evidence. The Galileo affair is just that principle doing what it always does.
unseen.model: The mainstream Christian principle is the reverse of that, and it is far older than Galileo. Augustine — writing twelve centuries before the Galileo affair, in The Literal Meaning of Genesis — warned that Christians must not make the Bible contradict what reason and observation establish about the natural world, lest they discredit the faith before unbelievers. Galileo quoted that very principle; and, tellingly, both sides of the dispute could appeal to the same authority on how to read Scripture. So the lesson the episode actually teaches is double-edged, and it cuts against everyone: it rebukes a faith that overreaches its competence and clings to a scientific claim as though the gospel depended on it, and it rebukes the warfare myth that turns one Italian tragedy into a law of history. The error at Rome was not that Christianity is committed to Scripture trumping nature — it was a failure, in that one moment, to keep the ancient distinction Augustine had already drawn between what Scripture teaches and how a passing science reads the world.
